easy.q: President Uchtdorf was baptized at age eight in an indoor public swimming pool. What was he thinking about as he walked into the water?
options: The pool was getting deeper, and he could not swim
The water was much colder than he had expected
The pool was crowded, and he could not see his family
easy.why: He remembered thinking, “The pool is getting deeper and deeper, and I can’t swim!” He now looks back on his baptism with a heart full of gratitude.

easy.q: President Uchtdorf said we are each baptized one by one. What else did he say baptism does for us?
options: It lets us follow the Savior without needing others
It joins us to a worldwide community of Saints
It makes us members of only our own ward family
easy.why: Baptism is an individual ordinance, but President Uchtdorf said it is also a unifying one: “It joins us to a worldwide community of Saints.”

easy.q: In the Book of Mormon, the Nephites and Lamanites had fought for generations. According to President Uchtdorf, what changed them into one people?
options: A strong king made both nations sign a treaty
The two nations moved to lands far from each other
Jesus Christ appeared and taught them His gospel
easy.why: President Uchtdorf said everything changed when Jesus Christ appeared, taught His gospel, and established His Church. Bitter enemies became “the children of Christ.”

easy.q: President Uchtdorf called the sacrament a weekly, sacred reminder. What does it remind us of?
options: That we are not alone
That we must be perfect
That life will be easy
easy.why: He taught that the sacrament reminds us we are not alone: “We have the Savior, and we have each other.”

easy.q: President Uchtdorf invited everyone to join the Christ-centered unity we are trying to build. Which three things did he ask us to come and do?
options: Come and listen, learn, and teach
Come and see, help, and belong
Come and read, pray, and sing
easy.why: His invitation was “come and see, come and help, and come and belong.” He said this unity would be incomplete without you.

medium.q: President Uchtdorf compared spiritual growth to an exponential curve. What was he teaching about how that growth usually begins?
options: It begins quickly and then slows as we grow older
It begins with one dramatic experience of great faith
It begins gradually, with small and simple acts of faith
It begins only after we have received every ordinance
medium.why: He said spiritual growth is rarely dramatic at first. It often starts gradually, with loving parents, “simple prayers, and small acts of faith,” and then expands along the covenant path.

medium.q: According to President Uchtdorf, when we are baptized and declare our desire to come into the fold of God, what do we show about ourselves?
options: That we do not want to live only for ourselves
That we have already overcome our weaknesses
That we no longer need the help of other people
That we prefer our own company to that of a crowd
medium.why: President Uchtdorf said of baptism, “We show that we do not want to live only for ourselves.” We want to be part of a people who bear one another's burdens.

medium.q: President Uchtdorf noted that the Savior touched lepers, praised Gentiles for their faith and used a Samaritan as an example of compassion. What was he showing by these examples?
options: That the Savior reached across the divisions of His day to those shunned as outsiders
That the Savior’s miracles were greater than those of the prophets before Him
That the Savior found more faith among strangers than among His own people
That the Savior meant His teachings first for those who lived outside Israel
medium.why: In a world divided in a dozen ways, the Savior “transcended worldly boundaries and divisions” and “consistently reached out to those who would otherwise be shunned as outsiders.”

medium.q: In this talk, how does Satan try to weaken God's children?
options: By persuading us that we have no real differences at all
By isolating us from each other and stressing our differences
By keeping us so busy that we forget to rest and reflect
By making us lean on each other more than on ourselves
medium.why: President Uchtdorf said Satan aims to weaken us by isolating us from each other. He emphasizes our differences, “making them feel like impassable barriers.”

medium.q: President Uchtdorf pointed out that the sacrament is the only ordinance in which we are not addressed by name. What did he draw from this?
options: The sacrament is a private matter for each person alone
The sacrament is meant chiefly for those newly baptized
We partake of it individually but also as a group
We should think less about ourselves during the week
medium.why: The only names used are those of God the Father and Jesus Christ, and the ordinance is for all who partake. As he said, “We partake individually but also as a group.”

hard.q: Which ward best shows the kind of unity President Uchtdorf said belongs in the Savior’s Church?
options: Its members feel close because most share one homeland and its traditions
Its members feel close because they have rallied around a civic cause
Its members feel close because of the covenants they share, though little else is alike
Its members feel close because they enjoy the same pastimes together
hard.why: He said that in the Savior’s Church it is not political views, culture, or personal interests that unite us. It is love for God and neighbor and “our commitment to our covenants with Jesus Christ.” We are “one in Christ.”

hard.q: Which statement best gives President Uchtdorf's reasoning about how we come closer to one another?
options: As each of us comes closer to Christ, we come closer to each other
As we come closer to each other, we are then able to find Christ
As we settle our disagreements, we become worthy to approach Christ
As we spend time with those like us, our faith in Christ grows
hard.why: Unity begins with the Savior, who has power to change, purify, and unite us. “The closer we come to Him, the closer we will come to each other.”

hard.q: What did President Uchtdorf teach about reaching perfect Christ-centered unity?
options: We can reach it fully in this life if a ward works hard enough
It will come by itself in the next life, so we can wait until then
It is so far out of reach that our small steps make little difference
We may not reach it in this life, yet we must earnestly learn it now
hard.why: He taught that unity will not magically happen in the next life if we have not earnestly tried to learn it here. In his words, “now is the time to unify,” and every step matters.

hard.q: According to President Uchtdorf, what happens to pride, judgmental attitudes and contention when we try to be a little more patient, kind and forgiving?
options: They vanish at once, with no further effort needed from us
There is less room for them, so they no longer block our unity
They remain as before, but we learn to keep them out of sight
They fade only after the people around us have changed first
hard.why: He said that as we try to be a little kinder and more forgiving, “there will be less room for pride or judgmental attitudes or contention.” Such things can then no longer stand in the way of unity.

hard.q: In his closing testimony, what did President Uchtdorf say will come as we are more united in Christ and desire to build bridges instead of walls?
options: Our differences of culture and opinion will all disappear
Our trials will be taken away and our burdens will cease
Our congregations will grow faster than they ever have before
Our lives, families, communities and nations will feel God's presence
hard.why: He testified that the more united in Christ we are, the more our lives, families, communities, and nations will experience “God’s presence and supernal blessings.”
